subject: Architecture
title: Le Corbusier: Love Him or Hate Him
description: A short lesson to help you apply Le Corbusier: Love Him or Hate Him.

hook.text: Le Corbusier called a house 'a machine for living in.' Many people found that terrifying.

buildup.text: He proposed demolishing central Paris and replacing it with identical concrete towers in a park.

discovery.text: His five principles — pilotis, free plan, free facade, ribbon windows, roof garden — defined modernism.

twist.text: Cities that copied his tower-in-a-park idea created soulless housing projects that bred crime.

climax.text: His chapel at Ronchamp broke his own rules — curved, sculptural, and deeply emotional.

punchline.text: He wrote the rules of modern architecture, then broke every one.

quiz.question: What did Le Corbusier famously call a house?
options: A sculpture you can live in

details.summary: Le Corbusier's Five Points of Architecture — pilotis, free plan, free facade, horizontal windows, and roof gardens — defined modernist building design.
details.whyItMatters: Le Corbusier is architecture's most divisive figure — simultaneously the father of modern design and the architect blamed for soulless public housing. Understanding his influence reveals why modern cities look the way they do, for better and worse.
takeaways: Five Points of Architecture defined modernist building design
His vision of towers in parks shaped postwar urban planning
Praised for design innovation but criticized for social impact

faq.question: What are Le Corbusier's Five Points?
faq.answer: Pilotis (columns raising the building off the ground), free floor plans (non-load-bearing walls allowing flexible rooms), free facades (exterior walls independent of structure), horizontal ribbon windows, and roof gardens.

faq.question: Why is Le Corbusier's urban planning criticized?
faq.answer: His vision of high-rise towers surrounded by highways and parks destroyed street life, isolated residents in anonymous blocks, and separated living from working and shopping.
